---
title: "Learning route and outcomes"
---

This is a complete first teaching draft for a new 7.5-credit Organic Chemistry 1.
The sequence below organises five weeks of study; your course's official
timetable and assessment instructions take precedence.

## What you should learn

1. Read molecular representations and identify functional groups and charges.
2. Explain properties and reactivity using polarity, resonance and acid–base reasoning.
3. Distinguish conformations and configurations and interpret simple stereochemistry.
4. Draw valid elementary mechanisms that conserve atoms and charge.
5. Predict selected substitution, elimination, addition, redox and carbonyl reactions.
6. Propose a short synthesis and justify conditions and experimental checks.
7. Use simple IR and one-dimensional NMR evidence to distinguish structures.
8. Record, calculate and communicate laboratory results in a reproducible report.

These are the teaching outcomes used to organise these materials. The formal
course syllabus specifies the approved outcomes and examination rules.

## Weekly rhythm

| Week | Units | Main work to keep |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Structures; properties/IR; acids and bases | Annotated structures, a property explanation, proton-transfer mechanism and ionisation plot |
| 2 | Conformations; stereochemistry; mechanisms | Newman/chair drawings, stereochemical comparisons, electron-flow diagrams and short conformer/ee calculations |
| 3 | Substitution; elimination/addition; alcohols/redox | Explained reaction predictions, competing pathways and checked reactant amounts |
| 4 | Carbonyl addition; acyl chemistry; amines/aromatics | Stepwise mechanisms, ester/amide comparisons and a TLC evidence table |
| 5 | Spectroscopy; synthesis/evidence; integration | Structure puzzles, a short synthetic route and a report linking claims to evidence |

Each lecture is planned for **45 minutes**, including drawing, prediction and
checking pauses. Slide counts vary with the chemistry. Some steps are quick;
worked mechanisms and spatial reasoning deserve longer. Use the pauses to
construct an answer, rather than watching the finished drawing appear.

Each study day has an [interactive chemistry exploration](demos/index.qmd),
linked directly in the left menu. Predict a change, try the controls and explain
the result. Use these short activities within a worked-example block or as
independent practice; they do not add an extra lesson to the timetable.

Plan substantial time for drawing and independent problem solving. Three
lecture units per week leave room for tutorials, practical work and revision.
The eight R activities occupy about five hours plus time to assemble reports
and recover from mistakes; they form a small part of the overall chemistry work.

## A textbook-independent practice route

Use the [25-day chemistry practice route](practice/index.qmd). Each lecture
unit supplies at least 20 non-R paper problems, with separate hints and worked
explanations; each of the ten consolidation days has at least 12 mixed problems.
That is at least **420 paper chemistry problems**, with additional self-checks
and the short R tasks. Core, transfer and challenge routes let you practise
at a realistic pace and return for revision.

The local explanations, worked examples, definitions and supplied data are
sufficient for these exercises. You do not need the textbook to look up an
unseen structure, figure, constant or question. The reading guide offers
optional supplementary explanations.

## Check your understanding

Before consulting an answer, record your prediction and reason. If you make a
mistake, draw the corrected structure or mechanism and explain what changed.
Being able to recognise an answer is a useful start; being able to construct
and defend it is the goal.

The self-checks and worked practice are formative. They do not establish
examination weightings, compulsory attendance rules or grade boundaries.

## What comes next?

This course provides a foundation for biochemistry even if you do not take
more organic chemistry. Organic Chemistry II appears as a recommended
7.5-credit chemistry elective in the locally researched 2027 programme plan.
It is a possible route to deeper synthesis and reactivity; its detailed
syllabus and final course code remain to be confirmed.
